zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the returned transcription follows this copy, not a normalized headword list.

lines.note: Muxu is explained by kazu nashi, without number, and glossed as countless. The scan has Cazu naxi, not OCR Cazuinaxi; no extra dotted i is present.
Numero completes the description as numberless. The final S. is an upright written-language label, outside the italic explanation.
This separate muxu means having no owner, as nushi nashi explains, and carries the upright Buddhist label Bup.; its period belongs with that label.
Muxucô denotes an immeasurably long span of aeons. Cazu caguirimo naicô supplies the Japanese explanation; both circumflexes and the bare i are retained.

runs.text: de contos de annos, ou ſeculos.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes “countless counts of years or centuries.” It explains the scale of the aeons rather than adding another headword.
Muyacu is explained as eki mo nai koto, something of no benefit. Deſne- begins the Portuguese adjective for unnecessary.
Ceßaria completes deſneceßaria, followed by “without benefit.” The historical ß-like type is retained rather than expanded to modern ss.
Muyacuna is the adjectival form with the same meaning as the preceding entry. Idem refers to uselessness or lack of benefit.

Muyen, explained by en nashi, denotes lack of support or orphanhood. The short two-stroke terminal mark is read as a worn hyphen in orfãoda-/de, not the OCR period; the historical spelling is not modernized.
De completes orfãodade. The additional sense, yue naku shite, is glossed as freely or without payment; the explanatory i, is italic and gra- continues below.
Ça completes graça, “free of charge,” contrasted with payment. Muyenni fodocoſu is the Japanese example of giving in this way.
The example is translated as giving or distributing freely. This completes the second sense of muen.
Muyenjo is a temple or hermitage lacking support. Tera is a Japanese word embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is printed in its italic type.
The temple has neither revenue nor parishioners or supporters. The lightly printed e in nem is retained within the clear Portuguese construction.
Muyenna is the adjectival form meaning unsupported or without shelter. The scan shows nn, not the OCR sequence mn.
The missing protection is specifically that of relatives and others. This completes the description of the unsupported person.
Muyo is explained by amaru koto nashi: having nothing left over or in excess. The absence of a vowel-length mark distinguishes it from the following Muyô entry.
Muyo, muqet expresses neither surplus nor deficiency. The repeated word begins with M, not OCR N, and the final bare t in muqet remains unexpanded.
Tar completes faltar: nothing is either superfluous or missing. The closing written-language label S. is upright.
Muyô is explained by mochiiru koto nashi, not using something, and glossed as unnecessary. The circumflex is visibly different from the unmarked Muyo above.
The gloss finishes unnecessary and adds lack of benefit. The two long-s characters of the divided adjective remain on their respective physical lines.
Muyocu is explained by yoku nashi, absence of desire, and specifically glossed as not being covetous. The historical Portuguese cubiça is retained.
Muyocuna describes a person without covetousness. Its adjective-forming na belongs to the headword, not to the Portuguese gloss.
Muyôna is the adjective meaning unnecessary or of no benefit. The scan has Muyôna rather than the spurious extra i of OCR Muiyôna; the circumflex remains.
Muzai is explained by tsumi nashi, without sin or fault. The upright S. marks written usage, separate from the italic Portuguese.
Muzan is glossed as compassion or pity. This older sense is read from the printed explanation rather than replaced by a modern dominant meaning.

runs.text: Peßoa, ou couſa pera ſe ter cõpai-

lines.note: Muzanna applies to a person or thing deserving compassion. The abbreviated cõpai- carries its tilde over o and continues below.
Xão completes the divided word for compassion, followed by pity for that person or thing. Both the tilde and the continuation’s lower-case x belong to the print.
Muzanni is identified as the adverb corresponding to the compassion-related adjective. Adu. is italic grammatical apparatus.

runs.text: Palaura com que ſe mostra ter piedade,

lines.note: Muzǒ is a word used to express pity. The caron belongs to the Japanese vowel, and the Portuguese description continues on the next row.
The phrase completes the expression of compassion for someone and ends with upright X., the regional label. Enlargement preserves a faint final o in compaixão, omitted by OCR.

runs.text: Peßoa, ou couſa que moue a com-

lines.note: Muzǒna describes a person or thing that moves one to compassion. The gloss breaks after com-, and the caron is retained over the headword’s o.
Paixão completes compaixão across the line break. The x is badly abraded, but its faint surviving marks and the complete gloss support this reading rather than OCR pui ào.
Muzǒni is the corresponding adverb. Its caron remains distinct from the circumflex in Muyô earlier in the column.
Muzuto is an adverb referred to Munzuto for its definition. The reference target is upright Japanese text following italic Vide.
Muzumuzuto is assigned the same adverbial meaning through Idem. This is the final dictionary line of the M section; the following marks are ornaments, not words.

zones.label: Column 1 closing ornaments
zones.note: A large floral tailpiece and a smaller symmetric typographic ornament close the M section. The provisional strings assigned to c1-l037 and c1-l038 were false recognition of these designs, not alphabetic text.

lines.note: The decorated N belongs to the following printed A., forming NA, the turnip entry. It spans six physical rows and is restored as an enlarged initial with a taller crop. Nabo, not OCR Nobo, supplies the Portuguese meaning.
Mu completes na wo tsumu, glossed as gathering turnips. The visible portion of the large N at the left belongs only to the preceding line’s headword.
This Na denotes a name or fame, distinct from the turnip entry. The beginning Na- of its example is printed beside the same six-line initial.
Na wo matdai ni nokosu means leaving one’s name to later generations. Enlargement supports matdaini, with i before ni, rather than OCR matdani; Dei- starts its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: xar ſeu nome, ou fama aos vin

lines.note: Xar completes deixar, leaving one’s name or fame to posterity. Vin continues into douros without a printed terminal hyphen.
Douros completes vindouros, future generations. Na wo tsukuru begins the next example, assigning a name, while the ornamental initial ends beside this row.
Ru completes tsukuru, translated as giving a name. Na wo toru then introduces acquiring a name or reputation.
The translation completes acquiring fame. Na wo shirusu begins the example of recording or writing one’s name.
After translating writing one’s name, na wo ushinǒ introduces losing honour or reputation. The initial v and caron are retained as printed.
The lost object is honour or fame. Na wo todomuru begins the contrasting expression for leaving or preserving one’s name.
Na wo todomuru is translated as leaving one’s name or fame. Na wo kuta- begins the contrasting example concerning damage to reputation.

runs.text: Perder do bom nome, ou menoſcabar a

lines.note: Su completes kutasu, glossed as losing a good name or diminishing fame. The printed Portuguese Perder do bom nome is retained without grammatical modernization.
After closing the damaged-reputation example, na wo aguru introduces gaining a name or honour. The translation continues its divided no- below.
Me completes nome, followed by honour. This closes the series of examples under the name-and-fame sense of Na.
Naba, alternatively qinoco, means mushrooms. The upright X. marks regional usage; italic No begins a contrast with usage in Cami on the next row.
Cami is the regional designation embedded in the Portuguese sentence. The text says that there, and more generally, the term is Cu-/ſabira rather than naba.
ſabira completes the Japanese reference word Cuſabira. The worn initial long ſ remains identifiable; this short row ends the regional comparison.
Nabe is glossed as a pot or pan. The source’s panela and tacho identify the vessel rather than its material.
Nabete is marked for poetic use and explained by oshinabete, generally. P. is italic here; the printed initial V and the tilde over e in Geeralmẽte are retained.
Nabeteno is the corresponding attributive expression for something common or general, again marked P. The nasal abbreviation is comũa, with the tilde over u.

runs.text: Fumo, ou felugem que està pegada

lines.note: Nabezumi denotes soot adhering to cooking pots, not OCR Nobezumi. The worn headword vowel is a. Enlargement shows a small grave in està; felugem and the provisional st sequence are retained.
Nas panelas identifies pots as the surface to which the soot sticks. This completes nabezumi rather than introducing the following verb.
Nabicaxi is the causative verb for making something incline or bend. The principal part aita is a historical form and remains literal.
Brar completes dobrar. The Japanese quotation concerns people adhering in obedience; the scan supports xitagai, with t, rather than OCR xiragai.

runs.text: macotoni fuqu cajeno cuſa qiuo nabica-

lines.note: The quotation compares that obedience with blowing wind bending grass and trees. Its physical division nabica-/ſuga is retained, as are the printed cuſa and qi forms.
Suga gotocu completes the comparison. Feiq. is an upright citation label; italic Lib. 1 identifies the book, and ſojei- begins the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: tarem ſe lhe os homẽs, era como vento que in-

lines.note: The people’s submitting to him is likened to wind bending vegetation. The scan joins como, not com o; the tilde over e in homẽs remains unexpanded.

runs.text: clina, & menea facilmẽte as eruas, & plãtas.

lines.note: The wind inclines and easily moves the herbs and plants. The final word is plãtas, with a nasal-abbreviation tilde, rather than the garbled OCR plilas.
Nabiqe means to bend, bring into submission, or overcome. The principal forms uru and eta remain part of the printed headword record.

runs.text: vencer: commummente ſe vſa com algum outro

lines.note: The entry adds overcoming someone and says the verb is commonly used with another verb. The historical doubled consonants in commummente are retained.
After stating that the verb combines with another verb, fiqi nabiquru illustrates moving or drawing someone toward an inclination. Vt, is italic apparatus.
The first example concerns inclining someone. Fito no cocorouo starts the next example, whose object is a person’s heart or disposition.
Iy nabiquru describes influencing through speech. The Portuguese translates moving or bending the heart, with co- continued below.
Ração completes coração; the person’s heart is moved by words. This closes the speech-related example of nabiqe.
Nabiqi is the intransitive counterpart, inclining or bending. The gloss reads Inclinarſe, with n, not OCR Inclirarſe; ijta is the printed principal form.
Kaze ni kusa, ki ga nabiku describes grass and trees bending in the wind. The comma after cuſa belongs to the printed Japanese example.

runs.text: & aruores ſe inclinão com o vento. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the bending of trees in the wind. Fi- begins the next example about a human heart.
Fito no kokoro nabiku is glossed as a person’s heart yielding or bending. The printed tono begins mid-word from Fi- on the preceding row.
ſe completes dobrarſe, with a person’s heart as the subject. This short continuation closes the figurative application.
Nabiqi xitagai combines yielding with obedience. The gloss reads Rẽdendoſe obedecer, with a tilde over e and final -cer, rather than OCR Rãdendoſe obedecor.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The a of the isolated far-right Nabu- is abraded; this is not an additional dictionary entry.
